title: Al-Kafirun: to you your way
hook: you have your way and I have mine (109:6)
carry: to you yours, to me mine

segments.voice: Yesterday: An-Nasr, praise and forgiveness at the moment of victory. Your line was win humbly. Day one hundred sixty-five.

Let's split the difference. You come to my thing this week, I'll come to yours next week. In most of life, that's how peace gets made: a little give on both sides. The leaders of Mecca, the commentators say, made the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ an offer like that. We'll worship your God for a year, and you worship our gods for a year. Everybody wins. Everybody calms down. The answer was a surah of six lines, and its last line is still quoted today.
screen: `LET'S SPLIT THE DIFFERENCE.` → `A YEAR FOR YOURS, A YEAR FOR OURS.` → `SIX LINES IN ANSWER.`

segments.voice: The surah opens: say, O disbelievers. Kafirun means those who reject; here, the Meccan leaders who made the offer. Then it turns in a slow circle. I don't worship what you worship. And you don't worship what I worship. And I won't worship what you worship. And you won't worship what I worship. The repetition is the point: it closes the negotiation from every side. Not now, not later, not in turns. Then the last line, in Pickthall's translation: Unto you your religion, and unto me my religion. Scholars hold two things about that line. First, it draws a clear boundary in worship. The Prophet would not mix his worship with theirs, even for peace; classical commentators read the surah as a declaration that worship isn't something you trade. Second, the boundary is drawn without a threat. It doesn't say: and so we will make you. It says: yours is yours, mine is mine. Some Muslims, especially today, read that line alongside another verse, in Surah al-Baqarah, that there is no compulsion in religion, as a basis for living honestly beside people who believe differently. Scholars have discussed how far that second reading goes; it's a live conversation. A hadith in Muslim says the Prophet recited this surah, with al-Ikhlas, in the two short prayers before the dawn prayer. One says who God is. The other says clearly where you stand, and leaves others their own place.
screen: `THE OFFER: TAKE TURNS WORSHIPPING.` · `NOT NOW, NOT LATER, NOT IN TURNS.` · `A BOUNDARY WITHOUT A THREAT.` · `WITH AL-IKHLAS, BEFORE DAWN.` · then, large: `TO YOU YOURS, TO ME MINE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one disagreement you carry, with someone whose view you really don't share, about faith, politics or how to live, and notice the urge to win it or to blur it. Try a third thing: let it stand, and say to yourself, this is theirs, and this is mine. Hold your ground, and still wish them peace.
Al-Kafirun. The disbelievers, the name of Surah one hundred nine, which ends: to you your religion, and to me mine. Today's word.
Your line: to you yours, to me mine. A boundary, drawn without a threat. One hundred sixty-five, in the books.

howItsDone: Many Muslims recite al-Kafirun and al-Ikhlas in the two sunnah units of prayer before the dawn prayer, as the Prophet did, and some recite al-Kafirun before sleep.

original.note: Arabic: the disbelievers, from the root k-f-r; the surah's first address.

trapdoor: what you thought: a surah that tells unbelievers off.
what it means: a clear refusal to trade worship, ending with a boundary and no threat.
what a scholar hears: the occasion (the Quraysh offer) is in the tafsirs; classical scholars stress the separation in worship; some modern readers pair 109:6 with 2:256.
